entities.historicalName: Ciudad de Manila, island of Luzon

placeContext.headerLine: Jurisdiction not yet researched in this pilot

role.text: In view because the ships of this Story came in here, and because the money line on the World map is drawn from here.
Two ships that sailed from the Philippines on 1 July 1573 reached this port in November 1573,
and the cargo listed at Mexico for them included silks and porcelain.
In April 1575 Governor Sande sailed from here for Manila with two ships.
In December 1573 the viceroy wrote that a ship built at this port was about to sail for the islands, and that he had no guns for it.
Morga, writing in 1609, names Acapulco as the port where a ten per cent duty on China goods was taken.
No primary Source we have read says the money sent west left from this port.
The marker shows present-day Acapulco, an approximate location; it is not a surveyed position for the port of 1573.

storyLink.text: Where the ships came in, in The port that had money to spare

entities.historicalName: Chinese merchants who sailed to Manila (Spanish sources call them "Sangleys"; Morga uses the word)

temporal.label: c. 1572–1573 · approximate
temporal.rationale: The relation dates the first ships only as "a year ago", counted from letters written at Manila in 1573 on a day it does not give. The sale of their goods is told in the same 1573 letters. This was a run of visits, not a dated act.

connection.directionNote: Spanish America to Manila to the South China coast, westbound across the Pacific. Directional; not symmetric.
connection.directionFigureText: Silver from Spanish America  →  financed  →  Chinese merchants trading at Manila

spatial.originText: Spanish America · not place-bound · Mexico named in 1576, money from Mexico in 1586, Mexico and Peru by about 1602
spatial.routeStatement: Money went west from New Spain to Manila. Governor Sande wrote in 1577 that reals, which are coins, came each year with the provisions until he arrived in 1575. Manila's citizens wrote in 1586 that rich men in Mexico sent large sums. In 1588 Governor Vera taxed the coin brought from New Spain. Morga, writing in 1609, says the king's chest in Mexico sent a yearly payment. No primary Source we have read gives the amount or the first year, and no Source names the ship. Acapulco is drawn as the port the Manila ships used (Sande sailed from there in 1575); no primary Source says the money left from it. The Potosí link is not yet researched. No primary Source we have read ties Potosí silver to Acapulco or Manila in the 1570s or 1580s.

connection.scholarlyStanding: Checked against modern scholarship on 2026-11-12. Flynn and Giráldez (1995), Atwell (1982) and von Glahn (1996) explain the Manila trade by China's demand for silver, and all three place the large flows after the 1570s. O'Rourke and Williamson (2004) and de Vries (2010) dispute that this trade was globalisation. They do not dispute the trade.

mechanismText.text: Spaniards at Manila wanted Chinese goods and had money to spare.
The viceroy expected, and later the governor and Morga said, that the Chinese wanted silver above other goods.
That money came from Spanish America: Mexico in 1576; 'wealthy persons resident in Mexico' in 1586; Mexico and Peru by Morga's time and about 1602.
Where in Spanish America it was mined is not shown. The Potosí link is not yet researched.
The money was what the Chinese took, and by 1589 they went through Chinese licensing.
This is how silver from Spanish America helped finance the Chinese trade at Manila. The Claims it rests on are listed beneath it. Several of them are one kind of voice.

participants.text: Viceroy of New Spain, who forecast that silver would be needed
Governor of the Philippines (Sande), who named Mexican silver as the draw
Spanish officials and merchants at Manila, who had money to spare
Chinese merchants, who brought goods and took the money
Manila citizens (1586 memorial) and a Manila lawyer (c. 1602)
Merchants of Mexico and of Peru, who sent money through agents
The Ming court, which licensed the Luzon trade by 1589

connection.evidenceIndependenceNote: Five Sources are cited in support. All are Spanish colonial writers: two Mexican officials reporting on the same ships, a governor, a judge and a Manila citizens' memorial. Most of them thought the China trade was a loss. The one Chinese source (SB07) is an imperial record from 1589 about licensing and silver taxes, not about silver coming in. Several citations are not several confirmations.

reverseDisclosure.body: Chinese goods to Spanish America is a different Connection. Whether the goods carried east by the galleon (silks, porcelain) changed anything in New Spain or Peru has its own mechanism and its own Evidence. It is not drawn here.

connection.reverseRelationshipNote: A separate Connection, not an inversion of this one. Chinese goods to Spanish America is not created in this fixture, has no id, no relationship type, no mechanism Claims and no Evidence. If researched, it gets its own record.

handover.privacyNote: This report goes by email to the site's editor through Web3Forms, a form service run from India. It is not public. Web3Forms says it keeps submissions for up to three years unless they are deleted sooner. To catch spam, it may send your IP address, and your email if you leave one, to the spam filters CleanTalk and Akismet. The editor also sees your IP address, in the email that carries your report. You will not be asked to tick a box. The editor keeps your report until it has been dealt with and for 90 days after, then deletes it, including the copy held at Web3Forms. To remove your credit or your data, choose "Remove my credit or my data" in the first question of the form, and say in "Anything else" which preferred name or email. Please do not include anyone else's personal details. A person reads the reports we receive. We aim to reply within a week if you left an email. Checking a Source can take weeks, because we read it ourselves, through a library. What you report cannot change the page by itself; only a Source we have read can. This is not a vote, and it is not the place to add a fact.

body: Select the Event on the map, or in the list beneath it, to open its Story.

This Moment is Manila in 1573: Chinese ships trading at Manila, around 1572–1573, and the one Connection this pilot explains — silver from Spanish America and the Chinese merchants at Manila. Acapulco, on the World map, is there to locate that Story. No Story has been researched for it yet.

gaps.statement: The Potosí link is not yet researched. Potosí was the biggest silver mine in Spanish America, and Acosta wrote around 1590 that a third to a half of its silver was never registered. But no primary Source we have read ties Potosí silver to Acapulco or Manila in the 1570s or 1580s.

segments.text: We don't yet know when the first silver was paid west to Chinese merchants, or where in Spanish America it was mined.
In 1573 the viceroy said silver would be needed,
by 1576 the governor named Mexican silver as the draw,
and in 1586 Manila's citizens complained that money from Mexico was pushing up the price of Chinese goods.
No primary source we have read records a payment, its size, or a mine.
The Potosí link is not yet researched.

How much silver crossed the Pacific around 1600 is disputed. Spanish reports of the time gave very large sums. Atwell (1982) says it is a matter for debate whether they can be believed. Von Glahn (1996) calls the yearly sum in those reports far-fetched, but says Manila's customs records greatly understate the real flow. None of these figures is for the 1570s.
